planting.note: Set container or bare-root plants in late winter while dormant, December through February in zone 7-9, so roots establish before summer heat arrives. Homebell is an early-season heritage rabbiteye, so it will begin flowering while frost risk still lingers; site it away from low-lying frost pockets. Interplant with another early rabbiteye such as Climax or Premier for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Homebell was one of the first named rabbiteye cultivars, released in 1955 by the USDA and University of Georgia's Coastal Plain Experiment Station in Tifton from selections of wild rabbiteye stands, the same program that produced Gardenblue and Tifblue that same year. It carries a moderate chill requirement of roughly 350-450 hours below 45 degrees F and ripens early, coloring in late May to early June in the Gulf South, ahead of most modern cultivars. Berries are light blue, small to medium, and softer-skinned than newer selections, with mild, unremarkable flavor that made it more valuable historically for earliness than dessert quality; it has largely been superseded by cultivars like Climax and Premier that ripen just as early with better fruit. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark and keep it paired with a second early rabbiteye for fruit set, since it is self-unfruitful like all rabbiteye types.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Cultivars
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Rabbiteye Blueberry Breeding History

planting.note: Plant dormant container or bare-root stock from December through February in zone 7-9 to let the root system settle before summer stress sets in. Gardenblue blooms midseason, so it usually escapes the worst late-frost losses that catch earlier ripening rabbiteyes. Grow it alongside another midseason rabbiteye, such as Tifblue or Woodard, to ensure good cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Gardenblue was released in 1955 by the USDA and University of Georgia's Coastal Plain Experiment Station in Tifton alongside Homebell and Tifblue, making it one of the earliest formally named rabbiteye cultivars. It needs roughly 400-450 chill hours below 45 degrees F and ripens midseason, typically mid-to-late June in zone 7-9, several weeks behind Climax or Premier. The medium-sized berries are a good light blue with fair flavor and were prized in their era mainly for the plant's vigor and heavy production rather than dessert quality, and the cultivar was widely planted commercially through the 1960s before being replaced by higher-quality introductions like Tifblue and Brightwell. It remains an option for gardeners wanting a tough, reliably productive heritage rabbiteye; set in acidic, pine-bark-amended soil and pair with a second midseason cultivar since it will not self-pollinate.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Cultivars
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Rabbiteye Blueberry Breeding History

planting.note: Set dormant plants from December through February in zone 7-9 so they establish roots ahead of summer heat. Because Menditoo is one of the earliest-ripening rabbiteyes, watch for late-spring frost during bloom in colder pockets of zone 7. Cross-pollinate with another early cultivar such as Climax, Beckyblue, or Aliceblue for a full fruit set.

directions: Menditoo was released in 1969 by the USDA and University of Georgia's Coastal Plain Experiment Station in the same batch as Briteblue, Delite, and Southland, and it was bred specifically to push ripening earlier in the rabbiteye season. Chill requirement runs about 350-400 hours below 45 degrees F, and fruit colors very early, often ahead of Beckyblue in zone 7-9 plantings. Berries are small to medium with a soft texture and only fair, somewhat tart flavor, which is why it was valued mainly for extending the front of the harvest window rather than for fresh eating, and it has mostly been dropped from modern nursery offerings in favor of Climax and Premier. Give it full sun and acidic, well-drained soil high in organic matter, and expect a productive but short shelf-life crop best used quickly after picking.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Cultivars
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Rabbiteye Blueberry Breeding History

planting.note: Plant dormant container or bare-root stock in late winter, December through February in zone 7-9, to establish roots before summer heat. Callaway flowers midseason, giving it more frost margin than the earliest rabbiteye cultivars. Plant with a second midseason variety, such as Woodard or Tifblue, since rabbiteye blueberries need cross-pollination to set a full crop.

directions: Callaway was released around 1970 by the USDA and University of Georgia's Coastal Plain Experiment Station, from the same breeding effort that produced Briteblue and Delite. It needs about 400 chill hours below 45 degrees F and ripens midseason, from mid-to-late June in zone 7-9, with medium-to-large berries of good light-blue color and better flavor than the older Homebell and Gardenblue selections. The bush is vigorous and upright with solid production, though it has been largely overshadowed commercially by later, higher-yielding introductions and today is found mostly in older home orchards and heritage plantings across the Gulf South. Grow it in acidic, well-drained soil heavily amended with pine bark or peat, mulch to conserve moisture, and pair it with a second midseason rabbiteye for reliable fruit set.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Rabbiteye Blueberry Cultivars
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Rabbiteye Blueberry Breeding History
